C’est dans l’optique de mieux comprendre: To better understand one of the Bloc Québécois's strategies, that of putting forward its vision of Québécois identity based on the French language and secularism, I took a close look at the party's election signs.
Le parti dit vouloir défendre les droits: The party says it wants to defend the rights of the province's residents, but does it truly represent the mosaic of its citizens? In the current political context, does the “we” put forward by the party work for everyone, or could it exclude Quebecers from immigrant backgrounds, or members of Indigenous communities?
Des commentaires que j’ai relevés sur le: Comments I came across on social media reflect discontent among some Quebecers with the signs in question, which read: “I choose French” and “I choose secularism.” So I set out to gather testimonies on the subject. My research paid off: I had the chance to meet a retired lecturer who used to vote for the Bloc Québécois. I found her testimony all the more relevant because she is also a doctoral student in religious studies.
Quant à l’experte avec qui j’ai discuté,: As for the expert I spoke with, I think she puts the party's strategy in context very well. Catherine Ouellet, a professor in the Department of Political Science at Université de Montréal, was able to break down the political news in terms of the factors I wanted to examine.

The parties use them to present their candidates in each riding. Among them, the Bloc Québécois signs caught our attention. The party is betting in particular on promoting the values it considers important when it comes to Québécois identity: promoting the French language and secularism. Dans sa plateforme politique, le Bloc pr: In its political platform, the Bloc proposes bills to “exclude Quebec from Canadian multiculturalism so that Quebec can choose its own model for integrating newcomers” and to be able to “firmly oppose the federal challenge to Quebec's Bill 21.” To better understand this approach, we spoke with Catherine Ouellet, a professor of political science at Université de Montréal.
Selon elle, la conjoncture politique jou: According to her, the political situation plays a major role in the Bloc Québécois's decisions.
« Depuis l’élection de Mark Carney à la: “Since Mark Carney was elected leader of the Liberal Party, the Bloc has plummeted in the polls in Quebec,” she notes. “According to the poll aggregator Canada 338, if an election were held today, the Bloc would go from 32 seats to 16.”
Ce recul place le parti dans une positio: This decline puts the party in a delicate position. All the more so since the central issue of this election appears clear: which of the Liberals or the Conservatives will be best placed to deal with Donald Trump's return to the American presidency?
« Le Bloc québécois se retrouve, de fact: “The Bloc Québécois finds itself, de facto, out of the equation,” the professor says. “It can't be the one to stand up to Mr. Trump.”
Ce contexte pousse le parti à adopter un: This context is pushing the party to adopt a more defensive stance, the researcher explains. Rather than trying to broaden its electorate, it is banking on the loyalty of its base. “The Bloc is consolidating the support it has always had,” Catherine Ouellet says. “Its partisan base is, by a large majority, made up of fervent defenders of Bill 96, Bill 21, and secularism.”
Ces thèmes, profondément ancrés dans l’i: These themes, deeply rooted in the party's identity since its founding in 1991, now serve as pillars of its election strategy.
